extracted.intended_audience: ML researchers, dataset creators, and practitioners working on vision-language models and multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmarks
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and constructing a purely-visual, multi-scene dataset (GSM8K-V) by converting text-based grade-school math word problems into images and establishing evaluation protocols for VLMs. Includes automated parsing, scene allocation, description templating, image generation, human validation, and evaluation/analysis pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem decomposition into (object, math value, semantic) triples
rubrics_metrics.description: Parse each textual GSM8K instance into a set of triples (object, math value, semantic) to form a structured mathematical representation for image construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an LLM parser (the authors use GPT-4.1) to extract object (entity), math value (numerical attribute), and semantic (contextual role). This structured representation is the systematic foundation for subsequent allocation, description generation, and image synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math information classification (13 classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize mathematical elements in GSM8K samples into 13 typical classes so they can be rendered in distinct visual forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map each extracted math element to one of the pre-specified classes (details in Appendix C.1). Each class has a corresponding visual rendering strategy to preserve the original mathematical information while aligning with realistic visual scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene allocation (1–2 math facts per scene) with allocation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate decomposed mathematical information across multiple scenes so each scene contains only 1–2 pieces of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow three guiding principles during allocation: (1) Contextual grouping — group information referring to the same object type, spatial setting, or functional purpose into one scene; (2) Final isolation — reserve the problem question for the last scene (contains no additional numerical values or objects); (3) Atomic fidelity — retain only atomic math facts (do not infer or merge values during allocation). The authors employ GPT-4.1 for allocation; see Appendix C.2 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce multi-dimensional interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally add controlled visual and semantic distractors to scenes to increase task difficulty and probe reasoning robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception interference: add irrelevant but visually salient objects. Semantic interference: add distractors contextually close to the math problem. These strategies make benchmark items more challenging and reduce shortcut solutions. Details in Appendix D.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta description strategy mapping and templating
rubrics_metrics.description: Map each math-information category to a corresponding meta description strategy with pre-specified prompts/templates used to generate scene descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design high-level templates (e.g., time & clock, percentage, measurement, signboard & icon) so generated textual scene descriptions preserve the mathematical intent. Complete templates and strategies are provided in Appendix D.2; these templates guide subsequent LLM-based description generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene description schema: object, action, composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce structured scene descriptions following a tripartite schema: Object, Action, Composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Object: concrete entities that carry math information; Action: state/activity that conveys semantic cues; Composition: spatial arrangement/positional relations. Use an LLM (GPT-4.1 in the paper) to generate these structured descriptions to ensure consistency for image generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-scene image generation specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate multi-scene images from structured scene descriptions using an image-generation model with specified resolution and prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors use GPT-Image-1 to produce 1024×1024 pixel images for each scene. Category-specific generation prompts are provided (Appendix D.3) to ensure reproducibility. Produce one image per scene; an instance may contain multiple scene images per problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human cross-check and iterative refinement loop
rubrics_metrics.description: All generated images must pass a dual human cross-validation process and be refined iteratively until they meet benchmark requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully trained annotators perform a two-person cross-check. If violations are found (consistency/completeness/compliance), images are refined; severe issues trigger manual correction of scene descriptions. Repeat the generate–verify loop until all problem–image pairs meet standards. Detailed cross-check protocols in Appendix C.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check principle — Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual scenes must faithfully preserve the entities, quantities, and constraints specified in the original text to ensure semantic equivalence across modalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During human validation, verify that every entity and numeric attribute in the textual source is represented accurately in the images — no missing or altered values that would change solvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check principle — Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: All information necessary to solve the problem must be visually accessible in the images without requiring extra assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure no implicit or external assumptions are required; if critical info was omitted or obscured, refine images/descriptions so the solver can proceed using only the provided visual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check principle — Compliance (safety & formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images must adhere to safety and formatting standards: exclude sensitive content, maintain clarity of object identities, and ensure legibility of numerical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators must flag and correct any safety issues, ambiguous object depictions, or illegible numbers. Compliance also covers style/formatting constraints enforced across the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve semantic fidelity for within-item cross-modal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct visual counterparts that preserve the exact set of problems as the text benchmark so models can be compared on the same item across modalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSM8K-V renders GSM8K problems into visual form without changing problem semantics; this allows clean within-item comparisons (text vs visual) to isolate modality effects on reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene granularity constraint: 1–2 math pieces per scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Each scene should contain only a small number of atomic math facts (typically 1–2) to isolate information and preserve reasoning order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This granularity helps VLMs track temporal/sequential dependencies and reduces confounding visual clutter; it's enforced by the allocation step and human checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset answer-type constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify and enforce answer formats for the benchmark (integer / decimal / fraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In GSM8K-V the Answer type is listed as Integer. During evaluation, models are instructed to output only the final numeric answer in the required format; prompt templates and format definitions are in Appendix B.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation instruction protocol: step-by-step with final numeric answer only
rubrics_metrics.description: During evaluation, instruct models to reason step-by-step over images but report only the final numeric answer in the required format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide representative prompt templates (Appendix B.2). The explicit instruction to output only the final numeric answer standardizes scoring and comparison across models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Input-mode ablation: implicit vs explicit question presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two input modes are considered: implicit (only images) and explicit (images paired with a masked question linking visual entities to semantics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly providing a textual mask or question linkage reduces ambiguity and yields slightly higher accuracy; evaluations should report both modes to measure the modality gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-image vs single-image input formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate models under multi-image (separate sequential scenes) and concatenated single-image settings since input format affects performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-image input tends to preserve temporal/logical order and gives slightly better accuracy; concatenation can obscure sequential dependencies. Appendix B.4 details input formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image style sensitivity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether visual rendering style affects model reasoning by testing multiple render styles (e.g., Pixar-style, Giphli-style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors chose Pixar-style for clarity; ablations show marginal performance differences across styles, but style-agnostic testing is recommended to ensure robustness (Appendix B.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality validation: test text-only, image-only, OCR, and caption inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate that the benchmark genuinely requires vision by comparing performance on text-only, image-only, OCR transcriptions, and structured captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR inputs performed very poorly (models cannot rely on text transcriptions), while caption inputs (structured scene descriptions) help but do not close the gap to text-only. Include these modalities in evaluation to confirm visual grounding requirements (results in Table 5 and Appendix B.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error taxonomy — Perception–Calculation errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and document errors where misperception of visual quantities or object counts leads to downstream calculation mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These errors are frequent when visually similar objects coexist or fine-grained details are required (e.g., count misreads, mismapping quantities to prices). Include representative cases and quantify prevalence (Appendix E.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error taxonomy — Instrument-reading errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and document errors arising from failures to read/interpret instruments (clocks, gauges, dashboards) used to encode numeric values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument-reading errors often break downstream arithmetic even when underlying math is simple; include case studies and analyses (Appendix E.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator training and human evaluation guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide thorough training for annotators, restrict tasks to objective judgments, and ensure fair compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should be trained to apply consistency/completeness/compliance checks and to answer problems directly from images. The paper states annotators received training and fair compensation and reported the task was manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements (hyperparameters, prompts, dataset/code release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Release all hyperparameter settings, generation prompts, templates, and dataset/code to ensure reproducibility of benchmark construction and evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors provide hyperparameters in Appendix B, generation prompts in Appendix D.3, and host dataset/code on GitHub and HuggingFace (links in the paper). Follow similar open practices for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline component specification and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the automated components used in the pipeline: LLM for parsing and description generation (GPT-4.1), image generator (GPT-Image-1), and inference frameworks (vLLM for open-source models; official APIs for closed-source models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document model versions, API usage, and inference/back-end frameworks so evaluations are reproducible and comparable. The paper details these choices and related appendices (e.g., Appendix B).
